'''Betty Shannon''' (née Mary Elizabeth Moore) (April 14, 1922 – May 1, 2017) was an American mathematician and the main research collaborator of [[Claude Shannon]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.technologyreview.com/s/401112/claude-shannon-reluctant-father-of-the-digital-age/|title=Claude Shannon: Reluctant Father of the Digital Age|last=Waldrop|first=M. Mitchell|work=MIT Technology Review|access-date=2017-07-26|language=en}}</ref> Betty inspired and assisted Claude in building some of his most famous inventions.<ref name=si>{{Cite news|url=https://blogs.scientificamerican.com/observations/betty-shannon-unsung-mathematical-genius/|title=Betty Shannon, Unsung Mathematical Genius|work=Scientific American Blog Network|access-date=2017-07-26|language=en}}</ref>

==Life==

Shannon was born on April 14, 1922<ref>Jimmy Soni and Rob Goodman, ''A Mind at Play: How Claude Shannon Invented the Information Age'', Simon and Schuster, 2017, {{ISBN|978-1476766683}}</ref> in New York City to Vilma Ujlaky Moore and James E. Moore. 
She was awarded a full scholarship to the [[Douglass Residential College|New Jersey College for Women]], where she graduated [[Phi Beta Kappa]] after studying mathematics.<ref name="ieee">{{cite web |last1=Yu |first1=Haizi |last2=Varshney |first2=Lav R. |title=On "Composing Music by a Stochastic Process": From Computers that are Human to Composers that are Not Human |url=https://www.itsoc.org/publications/newsletters/december-2017-issue |website=IEEE Information Theory Society Newsletter |publisher=IEEE Information Theory Society |accessdate=26 February 2019 |date=December 2017}}</ref>

She worked as a numerical analyst at [[Bell Labs]], where as a [[human computer|computer]] she supported work on microwaves, and then on radar. She published her own research on "Composing Music by a Stochastic Process";<ref>{{cite book |last1=Pierce |first1=John R. |last2=Shannon |first2=Mary E. |title=Bell Telephone Laboratories Technical Memorandum MM-49-150-29 |date=15 November 1949 |publisher=Bell Telephone Laboratories}}</ref> an "exceptional" accomplishment in an era when it was a "significant and unusual achievement for a woman to get her name on a research report".<ref name="ieee" />

While at Bell Labs she met the shy and insular [[Claude Shannon]]. Claude "didn’t have much patience with people who weren’t as smart as he was" and the two of them got on well.<ref name=si/> In 1948 he asked her on a date and they ended up dining each night together; they were married in 1949.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://news.mit.edu/2001/shannon|title=MIT Professor Claude Shannon dies; was founder of digital communications|work=MIT News|access-date=2017-07-26}}</ref>

In addition to her research, Shannon was a member of the Weavers' Guild of Boston, served as Dean of the Guild from 1976 to 1978 and received the Guild's Distinguished Achievement Award.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/bostonglobe/obituary.aspx?n=mary-elizabeth-moore-shannon-betty&pid=185382007&fhid=4277|title=MARY ELIZABETH MOORE "BETTY" SHANNON|website=Boston Globe|access-date=2017-07-26}}</ref>

Shannon had three children, Robert James Shannon, Andrew Moore Shannon, and Margarita Shannon, and raised their family in [[Winchester, Massachusetts]]. Her oldest son, Robert Shannon, died in 1998 at the age of 45. Betty died on May 1, 2017, at her home at Brookhaven in [[Lexington, Massachusetts]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=May 1, 2017 |title=Mary Shannon |url=https://www.douglassfh.com/obituary/mary-shannon |website=Douglass Funeral Home}}</ref>
